claim: Glycosyltransferases (GTs) are prevalent across the tree of life and regulate nearly all aspects of cellular functions.
source: Glycosyltransferases (GTs) are prevalent across the tree of life and regulate nearly all aspects of cellular functions.
evidence: This is a general statement about GT prevalence and function, supported by established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: A minimal core component is shared among functionally diverse GT-A fold enzymes.
source: based on deep mining of over half million GT-A fold sequences, we define a minimal core component shared among functionally diverse enzymes.
evidence: This claim is supported by the computational analysis of over 600,000 sequences described in the manuscript, which identified 231 aligned positions forming the common core.

claim: Variations in the common core and emergence of hypervariable loops extending from the core contributed to GT-A diversity.
source: We find that variations in the common core and emergence of hypervariable loops extending from the core contributed to GT-A diversity.
evidence: This is supported by the sequence alignment analysis showing three hypervariable regions (HVs) and variations in core positions across families.

claim: A machine learning classifier can predict donor specificity with nearly 90% accuracy.
source: Using evolutionary information encoded in primary sequences, we trained a machine learning classifier to predict donor specificity with nearly 90% accuracy
evidence: This is supported by the 10-fold cross-validation results showing the GDBT model achieved ~90% accuracy.

claim: Complex carbohydrates make up a large bulk of the biomass of any living cell.
source: Complex carbohydrates make up a large bulk of the biomass of any living cell and play essential roles in biological processes ranging from cellular interactions, pathogenesis, immunity, quality control of protein folding and structural stability (Varki and Gagneux, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Varki and Gagneux, 2019.

claim: Nearly 1% of protein coding genes in the human genome are estimated to be GTs.
source: Nearly 1% of protein coding genes in the human genome, and more than 2% of the Arabidopsis genome, are estimated to be GTs.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the proportion of GT genes in genomes, based on established knowledge.

claim: More than 2% of the Arabidopsis genome are estimated to be GTs.
source: Nearly 1% of protein coding genes in the human genome, and more than 2% of the Arabidopsis genome, are estimated to be GTs.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the proportion of GT genes in genomes, based on established knowledge.

claim: The GT-A fold is characterized by alternating β-sheets and α-helices (α/β/α sandwich) found in most nucleotide binding proteins.
source: The GT-A fold is characterized by alternating β-sheets and α-helices (α/β/α sandwich) found in most nucleotide binding proteins (Breton et al., 2012).
evidence: This structural characterization is supported by citation to Breton et al., 2012.

claim: The majority of GT-A fold enzymes are metal dependent and conserve a DxD motif in the active site.
source: The majority of GT-A fold enzymes are metal dependent and conserve a DxD motif in the active site that helps coordinate the metal ion and the nucleotide sugar.
evidence: This is supported by established knowledge about GT-A fold enzymes and is confirmed by the sequence analysis in the manuscript.

claim: Currently, 110 GT families have been catalogued in the Carbohydrates Active Enzymes (CAZy) database (accessed in February 2020).
source: Currently, 110 GT families have been catalogued in the Carbohydrates Active Enzymes (CAZy) database (accessed in February 2020) (Lombard et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a factual statement about the CAZy database content at a specific time point, supported by citation.

claim: Inverting GTs generally employ an SN2 single displacement reaction mechanism that results in inversion of anomeric configuration for the product.
source: Inverting GTs generally employ an SN2 single displacement reaction mechanism that results in inversion of anomeric configuration for the product.
evidence: This is established knowledge about GT catalytic mechanisms.

claim: Retaining GTs are believed to employ a dissociative SNi-type mechanism, where the anomeric configuration of the product is retained.
source: In contrast, retaining GTs are believed to employ a dissociative SNi-type mechanism, where the anomeric configuration of the product is retained (Moremen and Haltiwanger, 2019; Lairson et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Moremen and Haltiwanger, 2019 and Lairson et al., 2008.

claim: Most inverting GT-As have a conserved Asp or Glu within a xED motif that serves as the catalytic base.
source: most inverting GT-As have a conserved Asp or Glu within a xED motif that serves as the catalytic base to deprotonate the incoming nucleophile of the acceptor, and initiate nucleophilic attack with direct displacement of the phosphate leaving group (Lairson et al., 2008; Gloster, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lairson et al., 2008 and Gloster, 2014.

claim: The GT-A common core consists of 231 aligned positions.
source: The resulting alignment revealed a GT-A common core consisting of 231 aligned positions.
evidence: This is directly supported by the sequence alignment analysis performed in the study.

claim: The common core is defined by eight β sheets and six α helices, including three β sheets and α helices from the N-terminal Rossmann fold.
source: The common core is defined by eight β sheets and six α helices, including three β sheets and α helices from the N-terminal Rossmann fold (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This is supported by the sequence alignment and structural analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: Twenty residues are shared among diverse GT-A fold families.
source: Quantification of the evolutionary constraints imposed on the common core reveal twenty residues shared among diverse GT-A fold families.
evidence: This is supported by the conservation analysis of the common core alignment.

claim: The conserved residues include the DxD and the xED motif residues involved in catalytic functions.
source: These include the DxD and the xED motif residues involved in catalytic functions, and other residues not typically associated with catalysis (Figure 2A)
evidence: This is supported by the conservation analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: A conserved glycine at aligned position 151 (G335 in 2z87) is present in the flexible G-loop.
source: such as the conserved glycine at aligned position 151 (G335 in 2z87) in the flexible G-loop
evidence: This is supported by the sequence alignment and structural mapping.

claim: A histidine residue (H386 in 2z87) in the C-terminal tail at aligned position 207 is conserved.
source: and a histidine residue (H386 in 2z87) in the C-terminal tail at aligned position 207, henceforth referred to as the C-His.
evidence: This is supported by the sequence alignment and structural mapping.

claim: Residues from the G-loop in some families contribute to donor binding.
source: Residues from the G-loop in some families, such as the blood ABOs (GT6) and glucosyl-3-phosphoglycerate synthases (GpgS; GT81), contribute to donor binding (Patenaude et al., 2002; Empadinhas et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Patenaude et al., 2002 and Empadinhas et al., 2011.

claim: The C-His coordinates with the metal ion and contributes to catalysis in a subset of GTs.
source: The C-His, likewise, coordinates with the metal ion and contributes to catalysis in a subset of GTs, such as polypeptide N-acetylgalactosaminyl transferases (ppGalNAcTs; GT27) and lipopolysaccharyl-α−1,4-galactosyltransferase C (LgtC; GT8) (Fritz et al., 2004; Persson et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Fritz et al., 2004 and Persson et al., 2001.

claim: Fourteen hydrophobic residues are dispersed in sequence but spatially cluster to connect the catalytic site and the Rossmann fold.
source: The remaining core conserved residues include fourteen hydrophobic residues that are dispersed in sequence, but spatially cluster to connect the catalytic site and the Rossmann fold.
evidence: This is supported by the structural analysis of conserved residues.

claim: Eleven out of the fourteen hydrophobic residues are shared by other Rossmann fold proteins.
source: Eleven out of the fourteen residues (highlighted in yellow in Figure 2D) are shared by other Rossmann fold proteins (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) suggesting a role for these residues in maintaining the overall fold.
evidence: This is supported by structural alignment with other Rossmann fold proteins shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Three hypervariable regions (HVs) extend from the common core.
source: Our broad evolutionary analysis also reveals three hypervariable regions (HVs) extending from the common core.
evidence: This is supported by the sequence alignment analysis.

claim: HV1 is an extended loop segment connecting β3 strand and αC helix.
source: These include an extended loop segment connecting β3 strand and αC helix (HV1)
evidence: This is supported by the sequence alignment and structural analysis.

claim: HV2 is a segment longer than 28 amino acids connecting β6 and β7 strand.
source: a segment longer than 28 amino acids connecting β6 and β7 strand (HV2)
evidence: This is supported by the sequence alignment analysis.

claim: HV3 is a C-terminal tail extending from the β8 strand in the common core.
source: and a C-terminal tail extending from the β8 strand (HV3) in the common core.
evidence: This is supported by the sequence alignment analysis.

claim: The BPPS method partitions sequences into 99 sub-groups with distinctive patterns.
source: The BPPS method partitions sequences in a multiple sequence alignment into hierarchical sub-groups based on correlated residue patterns characteristic of each sub-group (Materials and methods). This revealed 99 sub-groups with distinctive patterns.
evidence: This is supported by the BPPS analysis performed on the sequence alignment.

claim: Fifty-three major sub-groups are defined based on phylogenetic placement.
source: Based on the phylogenetic placement of these sequences, we broadly define fifty-three major sub-groups, thirty-one of which correspond to CAZy-defined families (Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by the phylogenetic analysis and classification scheme.

claim: GT2 was sub-classified into ten phylogenetically distinct sub-families.
source: In particular, we sub-classified the largest GT family in the CAZy database, GT2, into ten phylogenetically distinct sub-families.
evidence: This is supported by the phylogenetic analysis of GT2 sequences.

claim: GT8 was classified into seven sub-families.
source: Likewise, GT8 and GT31 were classified into seven and five sub-families, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by the phylogenetic analysis of GT8 sequences.

claim: GT31 was classified into five sub-families.
source: Likewise, GT8 and GT31 were classified into seven and five sub-families, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by the phylogenetic analysis of GT31 sequences.

claim: Clade one groups four GT2 sub-families (GT2-CeS, GT2-CWR, GT2-Chitin-HAS and GT2-Bre3) with GT84 and GT21.
source: For example, clade one groups four GT2 sub-families (GT2-CeS, GT2-CWR, GT2-Chitin-HAS and GT2-Bre3) with GT84 and GT21 with high confidence, as determined by bootstrap values (see Figure 3 legends).
evidence: This is supported by the phylogenetic tree shown in Figure 3.

claim: Members of clade one are all involved in either polysaccharide or glycosphingolipid biosynthesis.
source: Members of these six families are all involved in either polysaccharide or glycosphingolipid biosynthesis.
evidence: This is based on known functions of these GT families.

claim: A conserved [QR]XXRW motif in the C-terminal HV3 is unique to members of clade one.
source: Additionally, the pattern-based classification identified a conserved [QR]XXRW motif in the C-terminal HV3 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2) which is unique to members of this clade.
evidence: This is supported by the pattern-based classification and sequence analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The [QR]XXRW motif residues coordinate with the donor and acceptor in a bacterial cellulose synthase.
source: The [QR]XXRW motif residues coordinate with the donor and acceptor in a bacterial cellulose synthase (from GT2-CeS family) (Morgan et al., 2013)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Morgan et al., 2013.

claim: Mutation of [QR]XXRW motif residues in bacterial cyclic β−1,2-glucan synthetase (Cgs, GT84) abrogates activity.
source: and mutation of these residues in bacterial cyclic β−1,2-glucan synthetase (Cgs, GT84) abrogates activity (Ciocchini et al., 2006)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ciocchini et al., 2006.

claim: GT8 sequences involved in the biosynthesis of pectin components group together in the GT8-GAUT and GT8-GATL families.
source: For example, GT8 sequences involved in the biosynthesis of pectin components group together in the GT8-GAUT and GT8-GATL families (Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by the phylogenetic tree shown in Figure 3.

claim: The human LARGE1 and LARGE2 GTs are multi-domain enzymes with two tandem GT-A domains.
source: The human LARGE1 and LARGE2 GTs are multi-domain enzymes with two tandem GT-A domains.
evidence: This is based on known structural information about LARGE proteins.

claim: The N-terminal GT-A domains of LARGE1 and LARGE2 fall into the GT8-Lrg subfamily.
source: Their N-terminal GT-A domains fall into the GT8-Lrg subfamily that groups closely with GT8-xylosyltransferase (GT8-XylT) subfamily enzymes
evidence: This is supported by the phylogenetic analysis.

claim: Fifteen out of fifty-three GT-A families are found in both prokaryotes and eukaryotes.
source: We further note that fifteen out of fifty-three GT-A families are found in both prokaryotes and eukaryotes.
evidence: This is supported by the taxonomic distribution analysis of GT-A families.

claim: The divergence of most GT-A families predates the separation of prokaryotes and eukaryotes.
source: These observations suggest that the divergence of most GT-A families predates the separation of prokaryotes and eukaryotes.
evidence: This is inferred from the phylogenetic distribution of GT-A families across prokaryotes and eukaryotes.

claim: The xED-Asp is nearly always conserved in inverting families.
source: In the inverting families, the xED-Asp is nearly always conserved and appropriately positioned to function as a catalytic base (Figure 4A)
evidence: This is supported by the conservation analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The xED-Asp is variable across retaining families.
source: The residue that acts as a catalytic base for inverting GTs (aspartate within the xED motif, xED-Asp) is variable across the retaining families consistent with its lack of role in the retaining SNi mechanism (Moremen and Haltiwanger, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by the conservation analysis and citation to Moremen and Haltiwanger, 2019.

claim: In GT43, the Asp base is replaced by a glutamate residue, which shifts the reaction center by one carbon bond.
source: For example, in GT43, the Asp base is replaced by a glutamate residue, which shifts the reaction center by one carbon bond (Moremen and Haltiwanger, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Moremen and Haltiwanger, 2019.

claim: Dolichol phosphate transferases (DPMs and DPGs) in the GT2-DP family lack the xED-Asp entirely.
source: Further, the dolichol phosphate transferases (DPMs and DPGs) in the GT2-DP family, which lack the xED-Asp entirely, transfer sugars to a negatively charged acceptor substrate (a phosphate group) and thus do not need a catalytic base to initiate nucleophilic attack (Gandini et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Gandini et al., 2017.

claim: In GT14, a glutamate serves as the catalytic base.
source: Out of these, only GT14 has representative crystal structures where a glutamate serves as the catalytic base (Briggs and Hohenester, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Briggs and Hohenester, 2018.

claim: Clade two groups inverting GT2-DPs with three retaining GT-A families (GT55, GT78 and GT81).
source: One strongly supported clade that includes both inverting and retaining families is clade two that groups inverting GT-A family members that transfer sugars to phosphate acceptors (GT2-DPs) with three retaining GT-A families that also have phosphate-linked acceptors (GT55, GT78 and GT81).
evidence: This is supported by the phylogenetic tree.

claim: Families in clade two share structurally equivalent conserved residues in the HV2 region that coordinate the phosphate group of the acceptor.
source: This placement is further supported by the observation that these families share structurally equivalent conserved residues in the HV2 region that coordinate the phosphate group of the acceptor.
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis and sequence conservation.

claim: In GT2-DP subfamily, R117, R131 and S135 in HV2 coordinate with the acceptor phosphate groups.
source: In the GT2-DP subfamily, R117, R131 and S135 (Figure 5A) in HV2 coordinate with the acceptor phosphate groups.
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: In M. tuberculosis GpgS (GT81), HV2 adopts a conformation similar to GT2-DPs.
source: Indeed, in the crystal structure of M. tuberculosis GpgS (GT81), HV2 adopts a conformation similar to GT2-DPs and the shared residues G184, R185 and T187 (equivalent to R117, R131 and S135) form similar interactions with the phosphate group of the acceptor (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Clade five places the inverting GT7 and GT2-CHS with the retaining GT27 and GT60 families.
source: Clade five places the inverting GT7 and GT2-CHS with the retaining GT27 and GT60 families (Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by the phylogenetic tree shown in Figure 3.

claim: GT7 and GT27 share structural similarities.
source: This supports the evolution of these families from a close common ancestor through gene duplication and divergence, which has been suggested through structural similarities between GT7 and GT27 (Ramakrishnan and Qasba, 2010b).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ramakrishnan and Qasba, 2010b.

claim: GT60 and GT27 families share a conserved mode of polypeptide Ser/Thr O-glycosylation.
source: The close placement of GT60 and GT27 families in this clade is also directly supported by previous literature indicating that these families share a conserved mode of polypeptide Ser/Thr O-glycosylation (Heise et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Heise et al., 2009.

claim: Each residue position within the core has been mutated in some context during the course of evolution.
source: Analysis of the patterns of conservation and variation in the common core indicates that each residue position within the core has been mutated in some context during the course of evolution, highlighting the tolerance of the GT-A fold to extensive sequence variation.
evidence: This is supported by the conservation analysis of the common core.

claim: GT27 and GT60 have replaced DxD motif with DxH motif.
source: While some of these variations are confined to specific clades or families, such as replacement of DxD motif with DxH motif in GT27 and GT60
evidence: This is supported by the sequence conservation analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: GT14 and prokaryotic members of GT6 have independently lost the DxD motif and no longer require a metal ion for activity.
source: For example, GT14 and prokaryotic members of GT6 that fall on different clades, have independently lost the DxD motif and no longer require a metal ion for activity (Briggs and Hohenester, 2018; Pham et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Briggs and Hohenester, 2018 and Pham et al., 2014.

claim: In GT-A families lacking the C-His, a water molecule coordinates the metal ion in a manner similar to the C-His sidechain.
source: Structural alignment of GT-A families lacking the C-His such as GT13, GT6 and GT64 families revealed a water molecule coordinating the metal ion in a manner similar to the C-His sidechain (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: In GT24, the C-His is substituted by an aspartate (D1427) which coordinates with the metal ion similar to C-His.
source: In other families, such as GT24, we found that the C-His is substituted by an aspartate (D1427), which coordinates with the metal ion similar to C-His (Figure 4B, bottom panel).
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: In GT15 and GT55, the conserved hydrophobic coupling between αF helix and the Rossmann domain is replaced by charged interactions.
source: Likewise, the conserved hydrophobic coupling between αF helix and the Rossmann domain is replaced by charged interactions (R388 and E274, respectively) in some retaining GTs such as GT15 and GT55 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Mutations within HV regions at aligned position 126 in the HV2 region (Y177A,G in 4lw6, GT7) have been shown to induce a shift in acceptor specificity.
source: Mutations within these HV regions, for example, at aligned position 126 in the HV2 region (Y177A,G in 4lw6, GT7), have also been shown to induce a shift in acceptor specificity (Tsutsui et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Tsutsui et al., 2013.

claim: Family-specific residues (R198, H221 and E224 in 5vcm) within the HV1 of MGAT2 (GT16) form a unique scaffold for recognizing the terminal GlcNAc of the N-glycan acceptor.
source: Likewise, family-specific residues (R198, H221 and E224 in 5vcm) within the HV1 of MGAT2 (GT16) form a unique scaffold for recognizing the terminal GlcNAc of the N-glycan acceptor (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The C-terminal GT64 domain of the multidomain EXTLs contain specific residues in HV2 (R181 and Y193) and HV3 (H289 and R293) that form a unique binding pocket for the tetrasaccharide linker acceptor.
source: Similarly, the C-terminal GT64 domain of the multidomain EXTLs contain specific residues in HV2 (R181 and Y193) and HV3 (H289 and R293) that form a unique binding pocket for the tetrasaccharide linker acceptor used to synthesize glycosaminoglycans (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The GDBT classifier correctly predicted donor substrates for 92% of the validation set sequences.
source: To further validate the model, we tested its performance on a validation set of 64 sequences that were not used to train the ML model but have known sugar specificities. The GDBT classifier correctly predicted donor substrates for 92% of these sequences
evidence: This is supported by the validation analysis of the ML model.

claim: 89% of the validation set predictions were predicted with high confidence.
source: The GDBT classifier correctly predicted donor substrates for 92% of these sequences, 89% of which were predicted with high confidence (blue rows in Figure 6—source data 2).
evidence: This is supported by the validation analysis of the ML model.

claim: Nearly 77% of the predictions have high and moderate confidence levels.
source: Nearly 77% of the predictions have high and moderate confidence levels and present good candidates for further investigation (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by the confidence analysis of predictions shown in Figure 6D.

claim: B3GNT9 is predicted to employ UDP-GlcNAc with high confidence.
source: B3GNT9 is predicted to employ UDP-GlcNAc with high confidence like other GT31 β−3-N-acetylglucosaminyltransferases (B3GNTs) in humans (Togayachi et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a prediction from the ML model, supported by comparison to known B3GNTs.

claim: The two procollagen galactosyltransferases in humans (COLGALT1 and COLGALT2) are multidomain proteins with two tandem GT-A domains.
source: The two procollagen galactosyltransferases in humans (COLGALT1 and COLGALT2) are multidomain proteins with two tandem GT-A domains.
evidence: This is based on known structural information about these proteins.

claim: The C-terminal domains of COLGALT1 and COLGALT2 catalyze β-Gal addition to hydroxylysine side-chains in collagen.
source: While their respective C-terminal domains catalyze β-Gal addition to hydroxylysine side-chains in collagen (Schegg et al., 2009)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Schegg et al., 2009.

claim: The N-terminal GT domains of COLGALT1 and COLGALT2 are predicted to have GlcNAc and Glc transferase roles, respectively.
source: our predictions assign a putative GlcNAc and Glc transferase role for their N-terminal GT domains, respectively.
evidence: This is a prediction from the ML model.

claim: GLT8D1 is implicated in neurodegenerative diseases.
source: More interestingly, GLT8D1, a GT8 GT with an unknown function implicated in neurodegenerative diseases (Cooper-Knock et al., 2019)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Cooper-Knock et al., 2019.

claim: GLT8D1 is predicted to have a glucosyltransferase specificity.
source: GLT8D1, a GT8 GT with an unknown function implicated in neurodegenerative diseases (Cooper-Knock et al., 2019), is predicted to have a glucosyltransferase specificity.
evidence: This is a prediction from the ML model.

claim: The most contributing features of the GDBT model include residues directly involved in substrate binding and catalytic functions such as the Asp within the DxD motif, residues in the G-loop, the catalytic base and the C-His.
source: As expected, some of the most contributing features include residues directly involved in substrate binding and catalytic functions such as the Asp within the DxD motif, residues in the G-loop, the catalytic base and the C-His (Patenaude et al., 2002; Empadinhas et al., 2011; Gandini et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by the feature importance analysis of the ML model and citations.

claim: Multiple residues from the alpha-C helix (aligned position 65–72; Y217-N224 in 2z87) are identified as key specificity determining residues.
source: Additionally, multiple residues from the alpha-C helix (aligned position 65–72; Y217-N224 in 2z87) immediately following HV1 are also identified as key specificity determining residues.
evidence: This is supported by the feature importance analysis of the ML model.

claim: Mutation of a single residue at position 67 in bovine β−1,4-galactosyltransferase T1 (R228K in 1o0r, GT7) resulted in relocation of the catalytic base and a change of donor specificity from Gal to Glc.
source: For example, Ramakrishnan et. al. showed that mutation of a single residue at position 67 in bovine β−1,4-galactosyltransferase T1 (R228K in 1o0r, GT7) resulted in relocation of the catalytic base and a change of donor specificity from Gal to Glc (Figure 7B; Ramakrishnan et al., 2005; Hancock et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ramakrishnan et al., 2005 and Hancock et al., 2006.

claim: Mutation of Y289 (position 149 in the consensus sequence) by a leucine broadens the specificity from Gal to GalNAc by creating additional space for accommodating the N-acetyl moiety.
source: Consistent with this observation, mutation of Y289 (position 149 in the consensus sequence) by a leucine broadens the specificity from Gal to GalNAc by creating additional space for accommodating the N-acetyl moiety (Hancock et al., 2006; Ramakrishnan and Qasba, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hancock et al., 2006 and Ramakrishnan and Qasba, 2002.

claim: A Random forest model trained using features from only the donor binding residues performs with an accuracy of only 75%.
source: Further, a Random forest model trained using features from only the donor binding residues performs with an accuracy of only 75%, indicating the importance of features other than those directly involved in donor binding.
evidence: This is supported by the ML model comparison analysis.

claim: The common core is present across all kingdoms of life.
source: Since the common core is present across all kingdoms of life, it presumably represents the minimal ancestral structural unit for GT-A fold catalytic function
evidence: This is inferred from the taxonomic distribution of GT-A sequences.

claim: The common core represents the minimal ancestral structural unit for GT-A fold catalytic function.
source: Since the common core is present across all kingdoms of life, it presumably represents the minimal ancestral structural unit for GT-A fold catalytic function by defining donor substrate interactions and minimal elements for acceptor recognition and catalysis.
evidence: This is inferred from the evolutionary analysis and structural conservation.

claim: GT function diversified through evolution of donor specificity by accumulation of mutations in the common core region and divergence in acceptor recognition through expansion of the hypervariable loop regions.
source: Based on our studies, we propose a progressive diversification of GT function through evolution of donor specificity by accumulation of mutations in the common core region and divergence in acceptor recognition through expansion of the hypervariable loop regions.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the evolutionary and structural analysis.

claim: Inverting mechanisms require an in-line attack and direct displacement by the nucleophile relative to the departing nucleotide diphosphate of the sugar donor.
source: Inverting mechanisms require an in-line attack and direct displacement by the nucleophile relative to the departing nucleotide diphosphate of the sugar donor and a conserved placement of the xED-Asp carboxyl group as catalytic base at the beginning of the αF helix.
evidence: This is based on established mechanistic knowledge about inverting GTs.

claim: Retaining enzymes generally alter the angle of nucleophilic attack by the acceptor, use a donor phosphate oxygen as catalytic base, and employ a dissociative mechanism for sugar transfer.
source: In contrast, retaining enzymes generally alter the angle of nucleophilic attack by the acceptor, use a donor phosphate oxygen as catalytic base, and employ a dissociative mechanism for sugar transfer (Moremen and Haltiwanger, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Moremen and Haltiwanger, 2019.

claim: Substitutions at the catalytic base may have served as a catalyzing event in switching between inverting and retaining mechanisms.
source: Since the main difference in these mechanisms is the change in position of the nucleophilic hydroxyl and catalytic base, substitutions at the catalytic base may have served as a catalyzing event in switching between mechanisms.
evidence: This is inferred from the phylogenetic analysis and conservation patterns.

claim: Inverting enzyme variants that accommodate changes to the xED motif group may represent examples of transitional phases in evolution between inverting and retaining catalytic mechanisms.
source: Thus, inverting enzyme variants that accommodate changes to the xED motif group may represent examples of transitional phases in evolution between inverting and retaining catalytic mechanisms.
evidence: This is inferred from the phylogenetic placement and mechanistic analysis.

claim: The clustering of mammalian N-glycan GlcNAc branching enzymes (MGAT1 (GT13), MGAT2 (GT16), and MGAT4 (GT54)) in the same clade suggests a common origin for these enzymes.
source: For example, the clustering of mammalian N-glycan GlcNAc branching enzymes (MGAT1 (GT13), MGAT2 (GT16), and MGAT4 (GT54)) in the same clade suggests a common origin for these enzymes
evidence: This is inferred from the phylogenetic tree.

claim: Placement of MGAT3 (GT17) in a separate clade could point to its unique role in adding a bisecting GlcNAc to the N-glycan core thereby regulating N-glycan extension.
source: while placement of MGAT3 (GT17) in a separate clade could point to its unique role in adding a bisecting GlcNAc to the N-glycan core thereby regulating N-glycan extension (Ikeda et al., 2014).
evidence: This is inferred from the phylogenetic placement and supported by citation to Ikeda et al., 2014.

claim: MGAT5 (GT18) involved in N-glycan β1,6-GlcNAc branching is a GT-B fold enzyme with a clearly distinct evolutionary origin.
source: In contrast, MGAT5 (GT18) involved in N-glycan β1,6-GlcNAc branching is a GT-B fold enzyme with a clearly distinct evolutionary origin.
evidence: This is based on known structural information about MGAT5.

claim: C1GALT1C1 (GT31, COSMC) shares a high sequence similarity to C1GALT1 (T-synthase).
source: Human C1GALT1C1 (GT31, COSMC) shares a high sequence similarity to another GT31 member, C1GALT1 (T-synthase)
evidence: This is based on sequence comparison.

claim: COSMC has lost both the DxD and the xED motifs and has no catalytic activity.
source: yet COSMC has lost both the DxD and the xED motifs and has no catalytic activity.
evidence: This is based on known functional information about COSMC.

claim: COSMC acts as an important scaffold and chaperone for the proper assembly and catalytic function of T-synthase.
source: Instead, COSMC acts as an important scaffold and chaperone for the proper assembly and catalytic function of T-synthase (Aryal et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Aryal et al., 2012.

claim: Over 600,000 GT-A fold related sequences were analyzed in this study.
source: Here through deep mining of over half a million GT-A fold-related sequences from diverse organisms

claim: The GT-A fold is the most common fold among glycosyltransferases.
